title: Gradient Descent on a 1D Quadratic

paper.title: An overview of gradient descent optimization algorithms

hook: Watch a ball roll down a parabola. With the right step size, it reaches the bottom quickly. With too large a step, it flies away.

explorations.title: Convergence for small learning rate
explorations.predict: Set η = 0.1 and x₀ = 1. Will the iterates approach 0?
explorations.observe: The series for x decays smoothly to 0. The loss decreases each step.
explorations.why: The update multiplies x by (1 - 2η). For η = 0.1, the factor is 0.8, so |x| shrinks by 20% each step.

explorations.title: Divergence for large learning rate
explorations.predict: Set η = 1.2 and x₀ = 1. Will the iterates converge?
explorations.observe: The iterates grow in magnitude and the loss increases rapidly.
explorations.why: The factor (1 - 2η) = -1.4 has magnitude > 1, so |x| grows by 40% each step.

limitation: This demonstration uses a simple 1D quadratic where the gradient is exactly 2x. Real loss surfaces are high-dimensional, non-convex, and may have saddle points or plateaus. The convergence condition η < 1/2 (for this f) does not generalize directly; in practice, the maximum stable learning rate depends on the largest curvature (Lipschitz constant) of the loss.
misconception: A common misconception is that a larger learning rate always speeds up convergence. Here, if η > 1, the iterates diverge. Also, η = 0.5 reaches the minimum in one step only because the function is a perfect quadratic; for general functions, convergence is asymptotic.

claims.text: The basic gradient descent update is θ_{t+1} = θ_t - η ∇f(θ_t).
For f(x) = x^2, the update simplifies to x_{t+1} = (1 - 2η) x_t.
With η = 0.5, the minimum is reached in one step from any starting point.

outcomes.outcome: Apply the gradient descent update rule to a 1D quadratic.
Explain how the learning rate affects convergence and divergence.
Verify that η = 0.5 reaches the minimum in one step.
